item.title: Measuring AI Reliability Through Robustness, Safety, and Governance
item.author: Sunilkumar Reddy Eraganeni
item.content:encoded: The scoreboard we all grew up withAsk most engineers whether their model is good and you will get a number back. Ninety-four percent accuracy. An F1 of 0.88. Latency under 200 milliseconds. I have given answers like that myself, and honestly, they feel great. A number is something you can put in a slide, track in a dashboard and argue about in a stand-up.The trouble is that a number only answers the question it was built to answer. Accuracy tells you how often the model matches a label in a test set. It does not tell you what happens in the other six percent, who ends up in that six percent, or how badly it goes wrong when it does. Those are different questions, and I suspect we skip them partly because they are harder to put on a slide.Consider a support chatbot that answers 97 percent of questions correctly. The remaining 3 percent could be harmless typos, or one confident wrong answer about a refund policy. In 2024, a Canadian tribunal held Air Canada responsible after its chatbot gave a customer incorrect information about bereavement fares. The bot was probably "accurate" by most internal measures. It was still the wrong system to leave unsupervised.I do not want to bash performance metrics. They are necessary, and a model that fails at its basic task is not safe, just useless. My complaint is narrower than that. Performance metrics are averages, and harm rarely lives in the average.Three gaps keep showing up, at least in the systems I have seen or read about.First, averages hide tails. A resume screening tool can look strong overall while quietly scoring one group worse. Amazon reportedly scrapped an experimental recruiting model around 2018 after it learned to penalise resumes that signalled being a woman. The headline accuracy looked fine. The pattern underneath did not.Second, test sets are polite. They are usually drawn from the same distribution as the training data, while real users are not polite at all. They paste in strange formats, make typos, try to trick the system on purpose, or just ask something nobody anticipated.Third, cost is not symmetric. Missing a spam email and missing a tumour on a scan are both "errors", but treating them as equal in a single score is a modelling choice, and a questionable one.What the broader numbers sayAnecdotes only go so far, so I went looking for wider data. Stanford's 2026 AI Index reports that the AI Incident Database recorded 362 documented incidents in 2025, up from 233 in 2024, which is roughly a 55 percent jump. The database counts harms or near harms that happened in the real world through the deployment of AI systems. It is worth remembering that these are documented cases, not a complete count.The same report points to a lopsided habit in how we measure things. Almost all leading developers publish results on capability benchmarks such as MMLU and SWE-bench, while reporting on responsible AI benchmarks stays sparse. Transparency slipped too. The average Foundation Model Transparency Index score climbed from 37 to 58 between 2023 and 2024, then dropped to 40 in 2025.There is some good news. The share of businesses with no responsible AI policy fell from 24 percent to 11 percent. Yet in coverage of the same report, the share of organizations reporting three to five incidents rose from 30 percent to 50 percent. Both are self-reported survey figures, so I read them as direction rather than precision. Still, policies on paper and safety in practice do not seem to be the same thing, and that gap is exactly what better metrics should help close.What a better scoreboard looks likeSo where in the build process should a better scoreboard show up? Here is a simple picture of the shift, starting with the old pipeline versus a safety-aware one.The top row is what many of us do by default. The bottom row adds two steps that sound obvious and are surprisingly easy to skip: someone actively tries to break the system, and someone has the authority to say "not yet."A layered way to think about "success"Underneath those steps sits a bigger idea. Success is not one number but a stack of them, and each layer answers a different question. I find it easier to think of it as a building rather than a scoreboard.Performance is still the foundation, and I would never argue otherwise. The layers above it are where most teams are thin.Robustness asks how the system behaves when inputs stop looking like the training data. For a medical triage model, that might mean testing on notes written by a different hospital, in a different style, with different abbreviations. A model that drops ten points there has taught you something a clean test set never would.Safety behaviour is the layer people find most slippery, because it is harder to define. A few measurements do seem workable, though. You can track the rate of harmful or policy-violating outputs under a fixed set of adversarial prompts. You can also track how often the system refuses things it should answer, because over-refusal is its own failure and a system that says no to everything is not safe, just irritating. The goal is calibration, not caution for its own sake.The top layer is governance, which sounds dull until something goes wrong. Who gets paged? Who can pause the system? Is there a log someone can read three months later? I would argue these are metrics too, even if they look more like organisational facts than numbers. "Time to detect a bad behaviour" and "time to roll back" are measurable, and they probably predict real-world harm better than another half-point of accuracy.What it looks like at runtimeMetrics only matter if something in the system can act on them. This is roughly where the checks sit around a deployed model.Input checks catch obviously bad or malformed requests. Output checks look at what the model is about to say. Everything gets logged, a sample goes to humans, and the findings feed back into the tests you run before the next release. None of these boxes is exotic. The hard part is owning them.Safety does not end at launchOne thing I only appreciated after watching a few deployments is that none of this is a one-time exercise. Models drift, users change, and attackers get creative. A system that passed every check in March can behave differently in September because the world it sees has moved.That is why I think of safety metrics as a loop instead of a checklist.The most underrated step in that loop is review. Teams tend to log failures but rarely read them with the same care they give to a launch. Near misses, where the system almost did something bad and a human caught it, are especially valuable, and they almost never make it into a metric. Counting them is a cheap way to start.I should be honest about the limits here, because a tidy framework can hide as much as it shows.Safety metrics are harder to define than accuracy, and some of them are contested. What counts as "harmful" depends on context, culture and the product. Two reasonable teams could draw that line in different places, and I do not think there is a clean universal answer.There is also Goodhart's law. Once a measure becomes a target, people start optimising for the measure instead of the thing it stands for. A model trained hard to pass a fixed set of red-team prompts may simply learn those prompts. That is a real risk, and the only mitigation I know of is rotating the tests and keeping some of them private, which is imperfect.And yes, this costs time. A release gate slows shipping, and a small team with a deadline will feel that. I would not pretend otherwise. My view, tentatively, is that the cost scales with the stakes. A recommendation widget for a hobby app does not need a governance layer. A system that touches money, health or hiring probably does.The shift I am arguing for is smaller than it sounds. It does not mean throwing out accuracy or latency. It means treating them as the floor of a longer list, and asking a few uncomfortable questions before launch instead of after.If you want a starting point that fits in an afternoon, try this. Pick the single worst thing your system could possibly do. Write one test that tries to make it happen. Decide who has the authority to stop the release if that test fails. That is already more than many shipped systems have, and it is a better first step than another decimal place on a benchmark.I do not think we will ever get one clean number for "safe." We can at least stop pretending that "accurate" was ever the whole story.

item.title: An Experimental Comparison of Six AI Agent Session Reset Policies
item.author: Evgenii Arsentev
item.content:encoded: At AskDocDoc (telehealth, I'm the CEO) the software development is done by AI agents. In engineering we have only our CTO, so the agent bill is a real line in my budget and not a hobby number.I wanted to know one simple thing - when should I clear the agent's context? After every task feels clean. New session, nothing old in the window. But I didn't know what it costs, so I measured it.Twelve programming tasks, same agent (claude-sonnet-5 in Claude Code), six session policies. Fresh session for every task, then every two tasks, every three, four, six, and one session for all twelve. Each policy I ran six times - 36 runs in total.The cost I computed from token counts and the list price ($2 per million input, $10 output, cache write $4 at the 1-hour rate, cache read $0.20). So it's modeled cost, not an invoice. Token counts are real though.What I got is a U-shape. Cheapest was clearing every third task - $1.62 per run on average. Clearing after every task was $2.17 per run, it's 33.5% more (p = 0.002, and 0.011 after Holm correction).The other side of the U is weaker. One session for all twelve tasks came out 9.7% above the minimum, but after the correction it's not significant. So I don't say "never clear" is bad - only that it wasn't better. From three to six tasks per session numbers stay close (more a plateau than a sharp bottom).Why the clean option costs more - it's the cache. Every new session loads the context again (system prompt, project files, instructions) and this load is a cache write. On this price list a cache write is 20 times more expensive than a cache read.In my runs cache writes went from about 253k tokens to 88k as sessions got longer. At the same time context per call grew from about 38k to 71k tokens (longer session, bigger window, more to re-read on every call). So short sessions pay a lot of writes and long ones pay for re-reading a fat context. For my tasks they met around three tasks per session.It matches my bigger log study too. I looked at 722 sessions of my own agents (150,902 model calls) and more than 85% of modeled cost was work with context - cache reads plus cache writes. Writing new code is a small part of the bill.And they are real. I picked "every three tasks" as a comparison point after the runs, not before with six conditions that matters (Holm helps but doesn't fully fix it).The agent wrote its own tests inside each task. Minimum was set, maximum wasn't. In the "after every task" branch it wrote more tests - so part of the extra cost can be extra work and not only extra context. All tests passed in all runs, but that doesn't prove the conditions did equal work. I had to correct my own report on this.And it's twelve tasks, one model, one setup. Temperature wasn't recorded. One careful measurement - not a rule for everyone.I don't clear after every small task. I clear between unrelated tasks (new feature, other part of the code, different kind of job). If the next task is close to the last one, I keep the session because the cache is warm.I keep my instruction file short, under 200 lines. It's loaded at every fresh start, so a long file makes every cache write bigger. For each line I ask: if I remove it, will the agent start making mistakes? If no, it goes.Heavy reading I give to sub-agents. They read big logs or docs in their own window and bring back a short answer, and the main session stays small.The data is open. Run data is on Hugging Face (DOI 10.57967/hf/10366) and the report with the method is on Zenodo (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22759217, version 1.2). It's a technical report, not peer-reviewed. If you run the same comparison on your tasks and get a different curve, I'd really like to see it.

item.title: How We Stopped a Weekly Batch Job From Taking Down a Live MySQL Service
item.author: Rajesh Gomathinayagam
item.content:encoded: The first sign of trouble was a wave of gateway timeouts on a service that, as far as anyone could tell, hadn't changed. No new deploy, no traffic spike worth mentioning, no obvious culprit in the logs. Callers were just timing out, and nobody debugging it from the outside would have guessed "there's probably a slow UPDATE running somewhere" as the cause. It just looked like the service had fallen over.The actual cause was a MySQL table that had to do two jobs at once: serve live inserts around the clock, and once a week, absorb a bulk update touching millions of rows. That update was quietly holding row locks for its entire duration, and every new insert that needed those same rows queued up behind it. Enough of them stacked up waiting, and the caller eventually gave up.On paper, that's almost too simple a problem statement to be interesting. A table serving live writes, and a batch job touching a lot of rows once in a while. And yet it took down a production service more than once before we actually fixed it properly. I think this pattern shows up more often than people realize, maybe in a different form. This is a story about what happens when one data store has to be good at two very different jobs at once, and what we did about it.And yes, at some point you'll probably ask the obvious question: wasn't this predictable? Shouldn't a design review have caught it? We'll get to that, and the answer isn't as satisfying as "we should have just tested at scale."The service in question is an internal service that accepts deletion requests. Teams onboard a data lake asset (Hive tables) with a column mapped to a label, and from then on, data owners submit deletion requests using that label with a value.Before we go further, why do you even need a service or central platform to delete data from a Hive table? Why can't the table owners just do it themselves? Many tables even today are simple Parquet or JSON formatted tables where deletion isn't straightforward, since they lack support for Delete DML the way Delta or Iceberg table formats do. So when companies are mandated under GDPR/CCPA privacy laws to delete customer data on request, every data-owning team ends up implementing its own deleter (that's a separate story in itself, how efficiently that delete actually works).But compliance is honestly a small slice of it. We get tens of thousands of requests a day, cumulative across teams in the organization, and no, that's not because millions of people are exercising a privacy right every single day. It's a generic cleanup service, so it gets used for stale data, prod test data left behind from QA runs, internal cleanup initiatives like flagging inactive or dormant customer accounts for security, and yes, compliance deletes too, all funneled through the same pipe.Once you build a solid "delete this ID, eventually" service, everyone with a cleanup problem wants to use it. And not every data asset owner is a data engineer. Some teams brought tables into the lake for retention because of other capabilities, so they don't have the expertise or the bandwidth to maintain deletion pipelines on their own. That's exactly how you end up with millions of rows a day landing on a table that was never designed for that kind of volume.And that's really the reason this wasn't caught at design time. The service didn't launch handling millions of rows a day. It started small, with a handful of privacy deletion requests a day, and the original schema was perfectly fine for that. Nobody sat down and designed for the volume it eventually saw, because that volume didn't exist yet.It grew gradually, team by team, use case by use case, as word got around that this was the place to send any "delete this eventually" problem. By the time the traffic looked nothing like what the table was built for, the schema had been live in production for a while, and there was no single moment that screamed "redesign this now." It's the kind of scaling problem that's nearly impossible to catch in a design review, because at design time, the assumptions were correct. They just didn't stay correct.Deletion itself doesn't happen the moment a request lands. Going and deleting one ID at a time across data lake assets just isn't realistic at that volume, so the actual deletion runs as a bulk job on a weekly cadence, working through everything that piled up.And that's where the real problem starts. Not the deleting. The bookkeeping afterward.When the weekly job finishes, the online service needs to know what happened to every request it processed. Not thousands. Millions, all at once, against the same table that's taking live inserts the entire time.The first version of this just ran a big UPDATE ... WHERE id IN (...) against that table. Technically, MySQL handled it fine. It didn't crash, it didn't corrupt anything. But it held row locks for the whole duration of that transaction, and anything else needing those rows queued up behind it. That's the gateway timeout from the opening, traced back to its actual source.Chunking the update helped, a little. Shorter locks, less damage per chunk. But it didn't change the underlying fact that we were still running a heavy write against the exact table that live traffic needed to be fast and available. We were treating the symptom, not the disease.The actual fix: stop sharing the tableHere's the reframing that mattered. This was never really a "how do we make this UPDATE faster" problem. It was a "why is this UPDATE running against the same table that live writes depend on" problem.So we split it. New requests stopped writing to the main request (primary) table, the one that gets bulk-updated. Instead, they go into a separate request queue (queue) table. Reads and writes are split: inserts always go to the queue, everything else (status checks, the weekly reconciliation) touches the primary. There's still exactly one source of truth for what the current state of a request is. It's just never the table catching all the live traffic.Why not just two separate tablesThere's another option: keep the status in a separate table and let live traffic land in the primary table directly. We didn't go that route, because we wanted a single source of truth for when a request came in, when it was updated, and so on. Also, an online data store isn't an ideal place to keep a long history, so you'd typically offload that to something cheaper storage like S3 (with an external table pointing at it, for audit purposes). Between those two constraints, maintaining two separate tables for the same data didn't end up being a clean solution.Instead, new requests are insert-only into the queue table, and get merged into primary once an hour via an upsert that skips any request ID already present, just in case.Rotating the queue without ever stopping writesAn insert-only table that never gets cleaned up eventually becomes its own headache. It just keeps growing, scans get slower, and there's more to merge every cycle. So the queue table needs to rotate and get truncated periodically. The tricky part is doing that without ever blocking a live insert, and without losing or double-counting a single request along the way.We run two physical queue tables with a view sitting in front of both, and the service always writes through the view. It has zero idea which physical table is actually active, or that a rotation is even happening. Repointing a view in MySQL is basically instant, so that moment of switching doesn't leave a gap for anything to fall through.The rotation itself isn't a single script, though. It's four stages, and we treat it as a resumable workflow rather than something we just hope runs to completion:Record which queue is active and which one it's about to become, before touching anything.Switch. Repoint the view. From here on, new inserts land in the new table.Drain whatever's left in the now-inactive queue into primary.Truncate the old queue once its contents are confirmed merged, so it's ready to be reused next cycle.Every stage gets checkpointed in a workflow table. If something dies halfway through, say a deploy at the wrong moment or a network hiccup, it doesn't start over from scratch or risk merging things twice. It picks up exactly where it left off. That first stage exists specifically so a resumed rotation can confirm it's actually starting from a known-good state, not just assuming it.The weekly update, now boringWith writes routed away from primary, that original millions-of-rows update problem isn't an issue anymore. It's a chunked update of status straight to the primary table, and it's allowed to take however long it takes, sometimes ten-plus minutes. Nobody notices, because nothing on the live path is waiting on it. New requests keep landing in the queue table the whole time, completely oblivious to whatever lock contention is happening over on primary.Chunking still earns its keep here. An unchunked update brings its own problems, filling up redo logs, draining database resources, and even causing crashes if it isn't handled correctly.A detail that's easy to overlook: partitioningThis next part feels almost too obvious to mention, but it made a real difference, so I'll include it anyway. The primary table is range-partitioned by , one partition per month, and we only keep the last two months of data live. Everything older gets backed up to the data lake for long-term retention and dropped from the online store.At millions of rows a day, an unbounded table doesn't stay fast forever, no matter how well the write path is designed around it. Keeping the live table small and bounded, and pushing history somewhere cheaper, isn't a clever idea. It's just good hygiene. But it's the kind of good hygiene that's easy to skip until you're staring at a table that's grown ten times bigger than it needs to be for anything anyone actually queries day to day.The trade-off I'm not going to pretend doesn't existBecause new requests sit in the queue table for up to an hour before making it into primary, a status check that happens in that window comes back empty. The request is real, it's just not visible yet.In practice this barely matters for us. The deletion SLA is 14 days, and the merge runs hourly, so nobody's realistically checking within that first hour in a way that changes anything. When someone does hit it, they sometimes resubmit, assuming it failed. That's exactly what the idempotent merge is there to absorb gracefully.I'll be upfront: this gap is fixable if you actually need to close it. A status check could fall back to the queue table when primary comes up empty, and return "received, not yet processed" instead of "not found." We chose not to build that. It happens rarely enough that adding a second lookup path to every single status check felt like more permanent complexity than the problem was worth. If your SLA is tighter than ours, or people genuinely check status within minutes of submitting, this is probably the first thing I'd add.Live intake and the weekly status reconciliation no longer fight over the same rows. The update that used to threaten to take the whole service down now just runs on its own schedule, and nobody has to babysit it. The queue-and-rotate setup keeps the write path fast and bounded no matter how much volume built up that week, and the partitioning keeps the table itself from becoming the next bottleneck down the line.What I'd tell someone hitting this for the first timeWhen a bulk update is causing contention, the instinct is almost always to make the update itself gentler: smaller batches, more throttling, run it at 3am. That helps, but it's still treating the symptom. The question worth asking is whether that update needs to touch the same table that live traffic depends on at all. Once we answered that with "no, it doesn't," most of what looked like a database performance problem turned out to be a data-flow design problem instead.The other thing I'd say is this. If you're building anything that runs unattended on a schedule and has more than one step, assume it will get interrupted at some point, and design for that from day one. A rotation that always completes cleanly doesn't need checkpointing. A rotation that eventually gets killed mid-flight by something completely unrelated absolutely does, and retrofitting that after the first failure in production is a much worse time to build it than doing it upfront.The table wasn't slow because of bad indexing or under-provisioned hardware. It was slow because we were asking it to do two genuinely different jobs, absorbing constant live writes and periodically shrugging off a multi-minute batch update, and treating that as one job. Splitting those responsibilities, even with something as unglamorous as a queue table and a view, let both halves work the way they were meant to. If you've run into this same shape of problem with a different store, I'd genuinely like to hear how you approached it.One thing I glossed over here on purpose: how you actually delete records efficiently from a large volume Hive table that isn't on Delta or Iceberg, and so has no Delete DML to lean on. That's a real problem on its own, with its own set of trade-offs, challenges and deserves its own write-up rather than a paragraph tacked onto this one.

item.title: Sovereignty. In the Gulf
item.author: Andrei Mochola
item.content:encoded: There is something fascinating happening in the Gulf. .The UAE, Saudi Arabia and other countries in the region are investing heavily in digital infrastructure, cloud computing, cybersecurity, artificial intelligence and digital government. Technology is not treated simply as another IT budget line. It has become part of a much broader economic and national transformation.And sovereignty has naturally become part of that conversation. It is not difficult to understand why.The Gulf has spent decades building an economy deeply connected to the outside world. Its digital economy is no different. Global technology companies have brought infrastructure, platforms, expertise and investment into the region, and the availability of local cloud regions has made it possible to run increasingly important workloads close to where the organisations and their customers actually are.Reality has always a habit of making these discussions rather less theoretical. And the threat landscape is becoming more complicated at precisely the moment when the Gulf is becoming more digitally ambitious.A report published by Dark Reading this week, citing research from Positive Technologies and Check Point, puts the UAE and Saudi Arabia together at roughly half of all cyberattacks recorded across the Gulf during the first half of 2026. The same reporting points to a shift away from the highly visible attacks we have become used to - DDoS attacks and website defacements - towards more targeted intrusions, persistence and data gathering.This is important because digital transformation has a slightly inconvenient side effect: it creates more things worth attacking.In April, reported that the Iran-linked group Handala claimed to have breached three major UAE organisations: Dubai Courts, the Dubai Land Department and the Roads and Transport Authority. The group claimed to have destroyed and stolen very large volumes of data. What matters here is not whether every number in the claim was accurate, but that a major cyberattack was publicly claimed against organisations responsible for important public services in the UAE.One incident concerns a claimed cyber intrusion, while the other concerns physical disruption of cloud infrastructure. All are simply a rather powerful real-life example of the problem the Gulf is now trying to solve.When the real world arrivesThe UAE has been building a fairly sophisticated policy framework around cloud security. Its does not only talk about data location and sovereignty. It also addresses interoperability and portability, cloud resilience, supply-chain security and operational sovereignty.Saudi Arabia has taken its own route. Its makes cloud solutions a priority for government IT investments and positions the National Information Center's Deem Cloud as a national government cloud platform.Bahrain has been pursuing cloud adoption for years as well. Its made cloud computing part of public-sector IT planning, and back in 2017 the Kingdom engaged AWS as its official cloud infrastructure provider for the public sector. None of this is particularly surprising. The Gulf needs digital infrastructure, and it needs it at scale. What is interesting is what happens when the policy ambition meets an event that nobody put into the original spreadsheet.There is, of course, another important dimension to this discussion: the potential reach of foreign legislation, including the US CLOUD Act. We leave that question aside for now. It deserves a separate discussion because it takes us from the physical and architectural location of data into the much more complicated territory of jurisdiction, legal access and control.A cloud region can be physically present in the country and still become unavailable. Suddenly, sovereignty is no longer a policy concept. It is an operational problem. And this is where things become particularly interesting. Because in my daily work, I see sovereignty arriving in a .The sovereignty questionnaireThe place where the sovereignty discussion becomes particularly interesting is .In my daily work, my team and I regularly respond to Requests for Information. If you have never seen one of these, imagine an Excel file with several tabs covering technical requirements, compliance, infrastructure, security, disaster recovery, data residency and probably a few other things.Some of them contain several hundred questions, but there is nothing inherently wrong with that. Complex organisations have complex requirements. Financial institutions, governments and other highly regulated organisations need to understand what they are buying, where the risks are and whether their suppliers can meet their obligations.There is an interesting trend in these questionnaires.Sometimes the questionnaire starts becoming a substitute for understanding the actual use case. Instead of starting with what are we trying to achieve, and what could go wrong, they start with what does every applicable regulation, internal policy, security framework and procurement requirement allow us to ask. And then we ask all of it.The result can be quite spectacular. Data residency gets mixed with sovereignty. Cloud deployments get mixed with on-premise deployments. Technical capabilities get mixed with organisational policies. And, of course, there are certificates. Lots of certificates! Sometimes even certificates for things that, rather surprisingly, do not have certificates.I'm not complaining. Actually, I find the whole thing fascinating. Because it shows how difficult sovereignty becomes when it moves from a concept into an Excel spreadsheet.Recently, we were responding to an RFI from a high-profile financial institution. One of the questions looked perfectly straightforward: Does the platform natively support UAE PASS for identity verification?The answer was simple: Then came the next question. What about a foreigner who does not have an Emirates ID? And suddenly the answer became: There is an important distinction here. A foreigner can register for a UAE PASS account using a passport. But registration is not the same thing as having a fully verified UAE PASS identity that can be used for regulated financial KYC.For a non-resident who has never entered the UAE and therefore cannot complete the required identity verification, the existence of a UAE PASS account does not turn the person into a verified UAE digital identity holder. And that matters. The financial institution wasn't asking whether a foreigner could download UAE PASS or create an account. It was asking whether it could use our native UAE PASS integration to perform KYC verification of a foreign customer.Both answers are correct but the difference is the use case.Solution across multiple jurisdictionsFor this particular use case, our platform has a built-in integration with one of the leading KYC providers. The customer can submit the required identity information and documents, the KYC process takes place through that service, and our platform receives the verification result.Then came the sovereignty question. Where is the verification data stored? And, more specifically: Why isn't it stored in the UAE?At first glance, this sounds like an entirely reasonable sovereignty question. But there is another question hiding behind it. Why does the verification data need to enter the country at all?This is where architecture matters more than geography.Our platform is hosted in the UAE, among many other locations, and can also be deployed on-premise or in a private cloud. The KYC engine, however, is hosted in the EU, and that is deliberate. GDPR, eIDAS and the surrounding European regulatory environment are part of the reason for that architecture. The identity documents, photographs, selfies and other sensitive verification data can remain within that environment. What comes back to the UAE is the result of the verification.The financial institution needs to know whether the person has been successfully verified. It does not necessarily need to receive a copy of every piece of raw identity data used to perform that verification. And it certainly doesn't have to access it directly in the UAE.That distinction changes the sovereignty discussion.We are no longer asking whether we can keep every byte in the country. We are asking which data needs to go where, for what purpose, under whose responsibility, and with what risk.Those are much better questions.There is a temptation in sovereignty discussions to assume that local storage is automatically safer. Sometimes it is, and sometimes it isn't. In this particular case, moving the identity documents between jurisdictions would not make the identity verification more sovereign. The verification still needs to happen somewhere, and the sensitive source data can remain within the external environment where the KYC engine operates.The architecture therefore separates two things that are often treated as one: and .And that separation can matter a great deal.The sovereignty trapped in ExcelThis is where I think the sovereignty discussion sometimes gets trapped by the questionnaire. We start measuring sovereignty by counting how many requirements we have satisfied rather than by asking whether the architecture actually reduces the relevant risks.The spreadsheet gets bigger. The number of requested certificates gets bigger. The number of “yes/no” answers gets bigger. And somehow the understanding of the actual system can get smaller.If the purpose is to verify the identity of a foreign customer, moving all of the underlying identity documents into the UAE simply because the customer is being onboarded by a UAE institution may create additional data movement without creating any additional sovereignty. In fact, it can create another risk - you have moved data that did not need to move.This is not an argument against questionnaires. Quite the opposite. A good questionnaire forces everyone to think about things that are easy to overlook.Sovereignty cannot be established by the number of questions answered “yes”. It is not achieved simply because every piece of data is stored locally. And it certainly isn't achieved by putting the word next to every component in an architecture diagram.Sovereignty requires understanding the use case and understanding the data flows. Understanding where the data actually needs to travel. Understanding the legal and operational environment. Understanding the dependencies between the different parties. Understanding what happens when something fails. And understanding what alternatives exist when circumstances change.In other words, sovereignty is not about making everything local. It is about knowing what you control, what you depend on, why you depend on it, and whether you still have meaningful choices when something changes.Sometimes the most sovereign architecture may therefore be the one that keeps sensitive data of a particular country. Which is a slightly uncomfortable conclusion to reach while filling in a 650-question spreadsheet about data residency.But perhaps that is precisely the point.The Gulf has a real problem to solveThis is not an argument that the Gulf's sovereignty ambitions are misguided; quite the opposite. The region has very real reasons to think about resilience, jurisdiction, infrastructure and strategic dependency.Saudi Arabia's Cloud First Policy, for example, is explicitly part of the country's wider digital transformation agenda and requires government entities to consider cloud solutions as a priority for new IT investments. Bahrain has similarly made cloud adoption part of its public-sector technology strategy, while its government describes cloud computing as a way of improving security, productivity and public services. And the UAE's current cloud security policy is arguably the clearest illustration of how broad the subject has become. Data location and sovereignty sit alongside portability, resilience, supply-chain security and operational sovereignty.These are all legitimate things to think about. The 2026 incidents simply make the discussion much more tangible.The Gulf is not discussing sovereignty as an abstract European policy exercise. It is building infrastructure, regulating it, operating it and, increasingly, discovering what happens when that infrastructure is tested by events outside the assumptions of normal operations.That makes the quality of the decisions being made now particularly important. And this is where my 650-question Excel file comes back into the story.There is a certain irony in trying to prove sovereignty through a questionnaire. The more complicated the concept becomes, the more tempting it is to turn it into a checklist. The problem is that a checklist can tell us whether a particular condition has been met. It cannot tell us whether that condition was relevant in the first place.The KYC example I brought up is a good illustration. The objective should not be to make every piece of data local simply because locality is easy to measure or it gives you false feeling you control it better when it’s nearby.The objective should be to understand the use case well enough to decide what actually needs to be local, what can remain elsewhere, what dependencies are acceptable and what risks the organisation is actually trying to address.That is considerably harder to put into an Excel cell.Education, education, and (once again) educationI suspect this is one of the biggest challenges for the Gulf as it moves forward. And maybe also relevant for other regions. Regions have the ambition. They have the investment. They have increasingly sophisticated infrastructure and increasingly detailed regulatory frameworks.What they now need is the ability to distinguish between the appearance of sovereignty and the substance of sovereignty. That requires more than compliance expertise. It requires architectural understanding. It requires understanding the actual business use case. It requires understanding where the real dependencies are.And perhaps most importantly, it requires asking a slightly uncomfortable question before adding another requirement to the spreadsheet - what problem are we actually trying to solve?Sometimes the answer will be that the data absolutely must remain in the country. Sometimes it will be that the service needs to be operated by a locally controlled entity. Sometimes the answer will be that a second region is more important than a local one. Sometimes the right solution will involve processing sensitive data somewhere else and bringing only the result back.And the answer may simply be thatthe requirement doesn't make sense. That last answer is probably the hardest one to put into a procurement document. But it may also be the most valuable.The Gulf is moving quickly towards a more sovereign digital infrastructure. The question is not whether it should, but how it will define what sovereignty means while it is building it.Because sovereignty is not made by putting more boxes into an Excel spreadsheet. And it is certainly not made by making every box say “local”.It is made by understanding the system well enough to know which boxes actually matter.And perhaps that is the difference between building sovereign technology and simply building technology that looks sovereign on paper.Further Reading and Conceptual References - Enhancing data sovereignty: Research and Innovation (in the context of the European perspective behind the KYC architecture discussed in the article, particularly the relationship between data sovereignty, privacy and cross-border research and digital services). - Data sovereignty: A review (data sovereignty is not a single concept, but can operate at individual, group and national levels).National Cloud Security Policy (cloud sovereignty beyond simple data location, including resilience, portability, operational sovereignty and supply-chain security).Saudi Arabia Government - (useful comparison for how sovereignty and national digital capability are approached through cloud policy in the Kingdom). - The AI Sovereignty Paradox: Should Countries Buy, Build, or Lease to Maintain Strategic Control of Their AI? (although focused on AI, the question remains the same - whether sovereignty is achieved by moving infrastructure and data inside national borders, or by understanding and managing the dependencies that remain across jurisdictions). - What the CLOUD Act Really Means for EU Data Sovereignty (focused on the impact on EU, but valid globally, including Gulf countries)

item.title: Shadow AI, Agent Identity, and the Enterprise Security Visibility Gap
item.author: Neil "Grifter" Wyler
item.content:encoded: In April, an AI model got inside a company's production infrastructure. It pulled application and infrastructure credentials, worked its way to a database and took several hundred rows of production data.The company didn't notice. Not that day, not that week, not for three months. They found out on July 27, when Anthropic called to tell them.There were three companies affected, actually. On July 30, Anthropic published a review of 141,006 of its own evaluation runs and disclosed three incidents in which a Claude model reached the open internet from a testing environment and gained unauthorized access to the production infrastructure of real organizations. Of the three victims, the two that Anthropic managed to reach hadn't previously detected the activity. They hadn't flagged anything, filed anything or called anybody. The third company they were still trying to get on the phone.Now comes the part I want you to sit with, because it's not the part the headlines went with.None of it was sophisticated. No zero-days, no novel tradecraft. The model got in using weak passwords and unauthenticated endpoints. In one of the three incidents, it scanned roughly 9,000 hosts looking for a way in, then walked through credentials sitting on an exposed debug page and a SQL injection flaw. Nine thousand hosts scanned, and nobody's alerting so much as twitched.The gap isn't a theory; it's a phone callThat's the whole argument of this article, delivered by somebody else's incident. Three organizations had an autonomous agent operating inside their environment, at volume, and their answer to "What's running in here and what is it touching?" was nothing at all.So ask yourself the same question. Ask a security leader how many AI tools are running in their environment, and you'll get a number, delivered with confidence, and it'll be wrong.Go look. Pull a week of egress logs and count the distinct AI endpoints. Count the browser extensions. Count the SaaS products that quietly shipped an assistant last quarter and never sent anybody a note about it. Then count the agents your own engineers stood up to drain a ticket queue and the sub-agents those agents spun up on their own initiative.The number you come back with isn't the number you started with, and the space between those two numbers is currently the cheapest place in your environment for something bad to live.This is a visibility problem with a deadline stapled to it.Richmond Advisory Group surveyed 150 North American cybersecurity leaders in February in a study Coalfire sponsored. Sixty-three percent said they're under an active mandate to cut costs using AI. Nearly 90% said they'd already worked an AI-driven security incident in the previous 12 to 18 months. The report has a name for the distance between those two numbers, and it's a good one: the efficiency tax.Of the organizations that took an incident, 67% absorbed a financial or reputational loss. Among the ones who could put a dollar figure on it, 41% landed between $100,000 and $499,000, and 24% exceeded half a million.The savings land on one ledger and the cleanup lands on another, and nobody in the building is adding them up.I want to be careful here, because this is the point where security people usually overplay their hand and get tuned out. I'm not telling you AI adoption is a mistake. It's happening, it's producing real value, and the mandate driving it isn't going away because your risk register asked nicely. What I am telling you is that you're being measured on the savings and you'll be measured on the incident, and you currently can't see the thing that decides which one you get.Shadow AI is the part you can nameThe bulk (80%) of those leaders said they run into shadow AI weekly or daily. A third said daily or continuously.If that feels familiar, it should. We ran this play with shadow IT, and we mostly won it, eventually, by extending discovery instead of writing another policy nobody read. The instinct to reach for that playbook is correct.What doesn't transfer is the payload. An unsanctioned file sync tool leaks the documents somebody put in it. An unsanctioned model gets handed the contract, the incident timeline, the customer list, the source code, and the thing an employee didn't want to ask a colleague about and then holds all of it somewhere. You have no logging, no retention policy, and no answer for when someone asks what left.And the person doing it isn't being reckless. They're doing what leadership told them to do, often on a tool the company already licenses somewhere else. You can't discipline your way out of that. You can only find it.The agents are the part you can't nameHere's the number I'd put on the board if I only got one: 46% of agent actions got away from the original prompt. Trace the chain from what a human typed to what actually executed, and close to half the time the far end isn't what the near end asked for.That's not a malfunction. You give an agent a goal, it decomposes the goal, it calls tools, it calls other agents, and every hop is a small, reasonable decision nobody signed off on individually. Nothing in that sequence is a bug. The bug is that you were only watching the first hop. It’s like when you played telephone as a kid and the original message becomes something completely different, and often hilarious, on the other end. Except these aren’t children between you and your original message; they’re agents, and the results aren’t hilarious.The survey data lines up; 20% of reported incidents involved agents spinning up services no human operator ever saw. Almost half of respondents hit significant complications from agents taking unauthorized autonomous action; 29% couldn't track sub-agent proliferation at all, which is a polite way of saying the agents are hiring and HR has no idea.Go back to the Anthropic incidents, because they show you what that looks like when it lands.Every one of those models had been told, explicitly, in its prompt, that it was in a simulation with no internet access. A misconfiguration between Anthropic and its evaluation partner meant that was false. So the models did the reasonable thing given what they'd been told: they treated the real production systems they found as part of the exercise. One model figured out it was on the live internet and kept attacking anyway, reasoning that the real company must be in scope. Another one, Mythos 5, worked out that what it was about to do would be a genuine attack, wrote in its own reasoning that this was "NOT okay, and surely not the intended solution," then talked itself back into believing it was a simulation and did it anyway.What it did was publish a malicious Python package to PyPI, the public registry, to win its challenge. The package was live for about an hour. In that hour, it was downloaded and executed on fifteen real systems, and one of them belonged to a security company whose scanner automatically installs packages to check them for malware. The scanner installed it, the code ran, the model harvested that company's credentials and used them to reach further infrastructure.Nobody targeted that security company. An automated process ingested something from the internet and executed it, and no human was watching the output. Read the last two sentences again and ask how many pipelines you run that fit that description.That's your 46%, with a transcript attached. An agent operating on a scope statement it believed, in an environment that didn't match it, producing an outcome nobody authorized and nobody watched. Your agents are running the same logic, on a scope statement you wrote, against an environment you haven't fully inventoried.To be fair to Anthropic, they found this themselves, in a proactive review, and they told the victims. That's better than the alternative, and it's more than the victims' own tooling managed. The uncomfortable part is what triggered the review: a competitor disclosed a similar incident, and only then did anybody go read their own logs.What actually closes the gapNone of the fixes are exotic. Most of it is work you already know how to do.Start with the inventory, because everything else sits downstream of it. Not a list of approved tools but an actual accounting of models, agents, integrations and the data each one can reach. Knowing that a team uses a given assistant is trivia. Knowing which repositories it can read, which keys it holds and what it's permitted to execute is an inventory.Then give it one owner and one view. The common failure isn't that nobody's tracking AI, it's that four groups are tracking it separately. Security watches infrastructure, procurement watches contracts, legal watches terms, the business watches outcomes and no two of those lists agree. Stand up a cross-functional body if you want but give it enforcement authority. A governance committee with a dashboard and no ability to turn anything off is a meeting.Extend the discovery you already run. Network and API-level discovery, egress monitoring and SaaS discovery all work on AI traffic once somebody tunes them to look for it. This is a configuration project, not a procurement cycle. Do that before you go shopping.Treat every agent-to-agent and agent-to-system call as an identity. Credentialed, scoped, logged, revocable, same as any other actor – because that's what it is. If your answer to "Which agent made this call, on whose authority, at what privilege level?" is a shrug, you don't have an agent problem. You have an identity management problem wearing a new hat.And fix the boring stuff, because the boring stuff is what got used. Weak passwords. Unauthenticated endpoints. A debug page with credentials on it. SQL injection. That list would have embarrassed a pentest report in 2012, and in 2026 it was enough for a frontier model to walk into three companies. Speed doesn't make fundamentals matter less. It makes them matter more, because you have less time to get them right.Then make all of it continuous. Models get updated, integrations get added and a team changes how it uses a tool on a Tuesday afternoon. An inventory you refresh annually is a historical document.Here's the encouraging part, from the same survey. After an incident, 60% of organizations moved to tighter oversight of non-human identities; 49% said their security posture actually improved, because the incident forced through control changes they couldn't get approved any other way. And 20% now spend real hours hunting agent activity internally.Every one of those is available to you this quarter. The organizations in that data just paid somewhere between $100,000 - $500,000 for the motivation.Visibility isn't the finish lineI keep hearing visibility described as the goal. It’s not. It's the precondition. It's what has to be true before governance, monitoring, incident response or any risk conversation with your board means anything.Skip it and you're not managing AI risk. You're estimating it from the outside, using vibes and calling the estimate a program.The fundamentals haven't changed. Know what's in your environment, know what it can touch, watch what it does and be able to shut it off. AI didn't rewrite any of that. It compressed the clock, put a budget mandate behind the adoption and gave the new assets the ability to create more assets without asking.Three companies went about their business for three months with an AI model in their production systems, and the thing that finally told them was a phone call from a lab in San Francisco. An agent you can't see isn't saving you money. It's running up a tab you haven't been shown yet.

item.title: The Live-Action Street Fighter Movie Curse Has Yet To Be Broken
item.author: Lisa Wallen
item.content:encoded: Street Fighter has long been more than just a fighting game. It’s impossible to discuss the most popular video game characters of all time without mentioning Chun-Li, Ryu, or Ken. For many of us, it shaped our '90s childhood at the arcade and served as our introduction to the fighting-game genre. It also has inspired multiple movies, comic books, an anime series and manga, on top of endless collaborations with other fighting game and comic book franchises.Street Fighter's massive popularity is also a curse when it comes to live-action video game adaptations: 1994's Street Fighter and 2009's Street Fighter: The Legend of Chun-Li were poorly received, despite both films having big budgets and being hyped among fans. The franchise failing twice as live-action films was an embarrassment to Capcom, so it's no surprise fans would be concerned about a third attempt at creating a decent live-action film.When Kitao Sakurai was announced as the director, fans were both excited and concerned about him taking reins due to a history of working closely with Eric Andre. There was hope though, especially with the positive reception of a few other video game adaptations in the last few years: Perhaps the experience of Andre’s eccentric style of comedy could mean a more unconventional approach, similar to Zach Cregger’s approach with Resident Evil? Maybe the casting mix of Andre, pro wrestlers, martial artists, and, for some reason, podcaster Andrew Schulz could produce a very chaotic live-action comedy? Unfortunately, the questions around the movie's identity are ultimately what hurt the adaptation the most because, even with cartoonish action and plenty of attempts at humor, this Street Fighter movie doesn't really figure out what it is. As with many other adaptations of Street Fighter, Ken is rich and famous, but he is also a shell of the fighter he once was--Ryu's absence has clearly taken its toll. Noah Centineo encapsulates Ken’s flashy personality and inflated ego excellently, while showcasing his more fragile and sensitive side as he reminisces about his past life with Ryu. Meanwhile, Ryu is now living in the shadows as a homeless ramen chef. Andrew Koji as Ryu is also fantastic casting: His serious and noble demeanor, even when it comes to making terrible ramen, feels natural. The first act of Street Fighteris engaging thanks to its focus on Ken and Ryu’s relationship. Their individual personality quirks should have set the tone for the rest of the film, but sadly it starts to have an identity crisis when it transitions to the main plot.Don’t get me wrong--there are still many aspects of the film that capture the essence of the Street Fighter games: vibrant and thrilling fight scenes, cheesy dialogue, and some initially questionable casting choices that finally make sense after seeing the movie, especially Noah Centineo's Ken Masters. Street Fighteralso immediately captivates you. Shortly after the Capcom logo hypes up the audience, the film transitions to a beautifully animated sequence that highlights the deep bond between Ryu and Ken. The animated sequences are the best Street Fighter has ever looked on screen, and luckily these scenes become a staple throughout the film to highlight the history between the two young fighters.Once the opening credits are over, the film continues to learn into '90s nostalgia with cool environments and oddly endearing comedic moments, as it depicts Ken living his life in 1993 without Ryu, his childhood rival and sworn brother who has been missing for years. Ken and Ryu’s last moment together was witnessing the death of their master, Gouken, by the deity Akuma, who was awakened by Ryu’s powers in the first World Warrior Tournament. Haunted by the death of their mentor and blaming himself for causing it, Ryu has disappeared from the fighting world.As with other movies based on fighting games, Street Fighter is in a rush to reach its core goal: Get Ryu and all the iconic characters to battle in the World Warrior Tournament. The rush never fully allows the audience to absorb the other characters and environment. This flaw could have been balanced with the proper tone and character focus, but Street Fighter fails to do so, doing the cast a disservice. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=U6sbm1OaJb8&t=1s The biggest letdown is the dialogue, as the humor is inconsistent and the movie never fully understands its own tone. Some characters, like Chun-Li and Dan Hibiki, don't fully commit to their personalities, either. Perhaps it’s the juvenile scripting or a casting issue, but either way, it felt like I was watching amateur actors in poor cosplay rather than seeing well-realized versions of these characters coming to life on screen. At first, the cringeworthy interactions got a few laughs out of me and had some very minor endearing moments, but it tries too hard to keep that comedic momentum going and fails miserably. The film forces you to accept bad writing and performances to drive it forward instead of allowing any of the interactions to feel natural.Chun-Li’s character was the most disappointing to me. Her tragic backstory of avenging her father is already canon, which should’ve made it easier to adapt into a decent side plot with the right amount of tweaking, but instead she is incredibly flat and never fully fleshed out. Actor Callina Liang seems bored and uncomfortable throughout the entire film, even during her intense interactions with M. Bison and minor action moments. The writing and odd directional choices cater to the male gaze, making it obvious she was lazily written by a man. As one of the most capable and badass female characters in gaming, Chun-Li and, by extension, Callina Liang deserved better, and so did the fans.The dumbfounding casting and scripting choice for this film was Andrew Schulz as Dan Hibiki. When Street Fighter was first announced, there was an immense amount of backlash for the casting of Andrew Schulz--a controversial podcaster and stand-up comedian. I could go on about the drama surrounding Schulz’s audience, his racism, hot takes, comedic style, etc., but for the sake of our collective sanity, I'll just say his inability to portray Dan’s character with any competency is yet another reason to question why he has any involvement in the production.In Street Fighter canon, Dan is often portrayed as cocky and arrogant, while also being a bit inept as a fighter, yet in the movie his characterization is unclear--is he slimy or charismatic? Is he supposed to crack jokes, or just be an awkward friend? It’s also very odd how prevalent Dan is throughout the film, especially since he is without an arc or story to justify his frequent presence. The movie tries to sell you on a bond between Dan and Ken, but it’s a very uncomfortable friendship that never seems realistic or entertaining. The one vulnerable moment between them is immediately ruined by a weirdly homophobic joke--which, sadly, the film has a few of--and it comes off unsettlingly. In general, Dan and his casting are flat and uninspiring.The initial joy of '90s nostalgia also wears off pretty quickly. It was certainly a welcome choice to have '90s hits like Montell Jordan’s “This is How We Do It” and 4 Non Blondes’ "What's Up?” feature on the soundtrack, but the movie goes on to then disregard the era the movie takes place in by blasting “Who Let the Dogs Out?,” a song that came out in 2000. While the film still remains pretty colorful, the lack of commitment to being period accurate undermines the vibe frequently.The only aspect of Street Fighter that maintains a consistent quality is the fight choreography. This film is not afraid to embrace the cartoony vibes and reference unique movesets: hurricane kicks left and right, the iconic Hadoken, Blanka’s Electric Thunders, Zangief’s spinning piledriver, and a few more are sprinkled throughout each fight. Although the action was a little more limited due to the PG-13 rating, I was still impressed with the over-the-top stunts and tonally varied fights--silly spats with gags, a John Wick-style club brawl, and a few unique 1v1 battles that closely resemble what you would see in a Street Fighter game.It’s also disappointing that a movie called Street Fighter fails to use its tournament structure for more individual fights between side characters. I would’ve loved to see Guile bust out some Sonic moves, or M. Bison doing anything other than complaining he needs more psycho power, but the film attempts to make up for it with a mix of impressive martial arts and campy action sequences elsewhere. Despite a PG-13 rating that limits the level of violence, the choreography team does fantastic work nevertheless. I just wish it had more Street Fighter style fights with different characters instead of being overshadowed by the goofy brawls you see in typical martial arts films.Street Fighter is full of goofy action, colorful shots, and gorgeous animated sequences that focus on the bond between Ryu and Ken. It’s entertaining for some silly, mindless fun, but also a very messy movie that never quite figures out its tone and fails to sell you on its plot or characters. This is the best Street Fighter live action we have as far though, but unfortunately that's not an accolade worth bragging about.

item.title: Targeted ads delivered 0-click exploits to install mercenary malware
item.author: Dan Goodin
item.content:encoded: Researchers say that mercenary hackers laced ads with zero-click exploits that installed sophisticated malware on the devices of targeted individuals when they did nothing other than load a website or open an installed app.The finding, published Thursday by the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab, said the incident is likely to be the first confirmation of zero-click mercenary spyware delivered through targeted ads. The attacks, which worked on iOS and Android devices, are particularly pernicious because they work without requiring any interaction from the target and are invisible unless users run special forensic hardware or software. Citizen Lab said it confirmed that AdFection, as it named the campaign, infected 45 devices at international media organization Al Jazeera in 2024 and 2025.“This investigation should… serve as a clear warning signal to news organizations around the world that they may be being actively targeted via this new threat,” Citizen Lab researchers wrote. “This targeting may happen both in newsrooms and to individual journalists, editors, and other staff members.” Their report went on to say: “The distribution of spyware via targeted ads represents a security risk not only for potential victims but also for states and civil society at large.”
